newsitem.title: USA: Clinton inaugural off to a cold start.
newsitem.headline: Clinton inaugural off to a cold start.

text.p: The 53rd U.S. presidental inaugural festivities began on Saturday in bone-chilling cold temperatures that kept down the size of crowds attending events on the Washington Mall, but not their enthusiasm.

President Bill Clinton, who takes the oath of office at noon on Monday, spent his day mixing business with pleasure -- hosting both a brunch and a lunch for about 500 friends and their families from Arkansas and his college years.
He also worked on yet another draft of his inaugural address, re-writing "a whole new beginning," according to White House spokeswoman Mary Ellen Glynn.
Hoping to craft a speech that will resonate with the nation and be remembered by history, Clinton used his weekly radio address to raise a theme he will stress on Monday.

"My fellow citizens, we must not walk alone into the 21st Century," he said. "This next week, as we focus on the inauguration and the future of our great country, my greatest hope is that we as Americans will continue to find strength in our diversity."

The official three-day celebration began with "An American Journey" festival on the Mall -- a wide stretch of land that reaches from the Capitol to the Lincoln Memorial -- and featured a variety of music, food and interactive technology.
Event organisers erected seven "heated" tents which for the most part were only slightly warmer than it was outside, mainly due the canvas blocking some of the wind.
The National Weather Service said temperatures remained in the teens (-7 to -10 Celsius) for most of the day, noting that wind-chill factors made it feel much worse.
The thousands who bundled up and turned out, however, seemed glad they came.
"This only happens once every four years. We didn't want to miss it," said Tom Wilson of Laurel, Maryland, who came to the Mall with wife, Chris, and their three small children.

At the tent called "Harmony Hall," a man wearing multiple layers of clothing topped by a white-hooded sweatshirt picked up a microphone and looked at the audience of more than 100 diehards sitting in the metal chairs set up for thousands.
"I don't know what to say," he told the audience, "but on behalf of everyone ... who has been working on this thing, we seriously admire you for coming here and sitting on those chairs."
A U.S. Army brass quintet then came onstage and performed compositions from the 1800s.

The most popular attraction proved to be the technology tent, partly because of the computerized attractions inside and perhaps because it offered the most heat. Vice President Al Gore paid an afternoon visit to the tent, inspecting its corporate displays.

At the food tents, with booths featuring such dishes as jambalaya, fried chicken livers, chicken teriyaki, couscous and Italian sausage and french fries, workers wearing hoods and earmuffs served the patrons.
The loneliest man at the American Kitchen tent was Drew Shack of Columbia, Maryland. The lemon ice he was selling was not a hot item.
"It's warmer in my freezer than it is in the tent," he said. "I'm serious. The freezer's set at 32 degrees (0 C). It's 26 (-3 C) in the tent."
"You take it out and it freezes like a rock," he said.
Saturday's public activities were to include a fireworks display, hailed by organisers as one of the most elaborate held in Washington, although it was to last only about 12 minutes.
On Sunday the Clintons will attend a two-hour invitation-only performance by a star-studded cast ranging from singers Stevie Wonder and Aretha Franklin to the casts of several Broadway muscials.
After the formal inaugural ceremonies, Clinton will lead the traditional parade down Pennsylvania Ave. and attend a total of 15 formal balls at night.
